title: A 194-Year-Old Tortoise and the Secrets in His DNA
summary:
Jonathan the giant tortoise is about 194 years old, and scientists think his DNA may hold clues to why he has lived so long. He is an Aldabra giant tortoise, believed to have hatched in 1832. That means he was alive during the lifetimes of Charles Darwin and Queen Victoria. Today he is the oldest living giant tortoise and the oldest known living land animal.

In a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants linked to protection against aging. These variants influence several essential processes, including repairing damaged DNA, limiting inflammation, controlling insulin activity, and suppressing cancer. In other words, Jonathan's body seems to carry built-in tools for staying healthy.

One of the most surprising findings came from his epigenome, the system of chemical markers that helps decide which genes are switched on or off. These markers usually change as animals age, and those changes can disturb important cellular processes. But when researchers compared Jonathan's epigenome with those of younger giant tortoises of the same species, they found that the regulators involved in DNA repair and metabolism had stayed remarkably stable.

Dr. Justin Gerlach of the University of Cambridge, who took part in the study, said the gene regulators involved in energy production and DNA repair have remained incredibly stable in Jonathan over almost two centuries. He added that working with such an old tortoise feels like collaborating with a partner.

The research team, led by the nonprofit Kallel, hopes the findings could one day help scientists develop new ways to slow age-related decline and prevent chronic diseases in people. Turning tortoise biology into human treatments will require much more research, but the researchers believe nature has already found remarkable ways to handle aging.
why_it_matters: Aging affects every living thing, including people, so understanding how a tortoise stays healthy for nearly 200 years could one day point scientists toward new ways to slow age-related decline and prevent chronic diseases in people.

background_read: DNA is the set of instructions inside every living thing that tells its body how to grow, work, and repair itself.

Giant tortoises are famous for living a very long time, and Jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise believed to have hatched in 1832, which means he was alive during the lifetimes of Charles Darwin and Queen Victoria.
As animals age, their DNA can get damaged and the chemical markers that switch genes on and off usually change, which can disturb important processes in the body.
Scientists study very old animals like Jonathan because their bodies may carry natural ways of staying healthy, and learning how those ways work could one day help people age better too.
